appraisal_events.evidence: Gilberte grants him her first name (« vous pouvez m’appeler Gilberte ») and pronounces his own with pleasure and gratitude, but « au moment même, je ne pouvais apprécier la valeur de ces plaisirs nouveaux » ; she « me faisait aussi de la peine en ayant l’air de ne pas avoir de plaisir à me voir », he waits and fails to find her (« aux Champs-Élysées je ne trouvais pas Gilberte »), blames himself (« c’était ma faute »), and is shut out of « toute son autre existence qui m’échappait ».
appraisal_events.explanation: A real intimacy is conferred at the outset, but the narrator's own retrospective voice cancels its value and organizes the rest of the passage around anxious waiting, self-blame, and exclusion from Gilberte's inaccessible life, so the dominant local movement is a qualified diminishment of the narrator rather than a realized renewal.

appraisal_events.evidence: « Ses relations avec le comte de Paris... prenaient maintenant pour moi quelque chose de merveilleux » ; they « le faisaient se détacher vivement sur le fond vulgaire des promeneurs », he is likened to « un personnage historique », admired for consenting to appear among them « sans réclamer d’eux d’égards spéciaux, tant était profond l’incognito dont il était enveloppé », and he pays for his iron chair « de cette main que Philippe VII avait si souvent retenue dans la sienne ».
appraisal_events.explanation: Swann is sharply elevated by his royal connection and by an incognito the narrator openly admires; the closing image monumentalizes even his most banal gesture through contact with Philippe VII.

status_effects.explanation: Swann's local standing rises markedly: he is detached from the vulgar crowd as a quasi-historical figure whose intimacy with the Orléans is unknown to those around him.

The narrator ends locally weaker: the intimacy he receives cannot be enjoyed, Gilberte's apparent indifference and absence wound him, and he is left dependent on her unpredictable appearances and ashamed before Swann.
Gilberte holds the leverage: she alone decides when to confer the first name, when to appear, and how much of her life to disclose, and her mystery governs the narrator's whole afternoon.

ambiguities: Swann's elevation is filtered through a love-transfigured perception the narrator himself relativizes (« que j’avais vu si souvent autrefois sans qu’il excitât ma curiosité ») ; read as retrospective irony rather than endorsement, E2's effect would soften from +2 to +1. The reading here treats the prestige as factually grounded (the Orléans connection, Philippe VII) and the framing as admiring.

« Philippe VII » is taken to designate the same man as « le comte de Paris » (the Orleanist pretender), so E2 has a single prestige source; if read as two distinct figures the direction of the event is unchanged.
